I can tell you that with beer specifically hops are nearly always an ingredient (even in beers that don't taste "hoppy" like IPAs do), and they do have somewhat of psychotropic effect.. Honestly, I think it is more situational and psychologically based. Hops and other ingredients don't have the effect you are talking about. Plus, consumption rates have a great influence on intoxication, as does location.

When you drink familiar beers, or other beverages, in a familiar setting, your body and mind become accustomed to the situation and you can consume more. When you are put into social, and/or unfamiliar situations it takes you out of that sweet spot, which also adds to the effects of intoxication--often leading to greater feelings of intoxication with less overall consumption. This has been documented in heroin addicts that overdose. It's psychologically based rather than physiologically based--at least to a certain degree. Also, just the perceived newness can add to the effect; it is something new.

Socialization also (usually) leads to increased feelings of intoxication through greater consumption. People also tend to eat less during these periods, adding to the effect.

Considering that most spirits are made using the same ingredients these days, at the same locations, with a few differences in coloration and flavor, and the fact that the same thing can be observed using this example, it seems to be more plausible that location, situation, socialization, consumption, food consumption, fluid consumption, familiarity, elevation (but not due to alcohol blood levels), and overall "newness" is a much more likely candidate for the what @Tinker_Bell is talking about.
